Purpose: A short, friendly walkthrough that explains how Claude, MCP, and skills fit together — the fastest way to get oriented if you're brand new.
When to Use: Say things like “I'm new here,” “onboard me,” or “explain how this works” — or just ask when you're confused about MCP or skills.
Where to Use: Anywhere, for anyone starting out — developers, PMs, designers, support, sales, or data roles.
How to Use: Type /start, or just say you're new — Claude will pick it up automatically.
Input Requirements: Just answer two quick questions: your role, and whether you've used AI tools like this before. Nothing else needed.
Expected Output: A short interactive lesson, right in the chat. If you want, it can also save you a one-page cheat sheet and a completion summary — but only after you say yes. At the end, it'll also mention /new-joinee as an optional next step if you want deeper, role-specific onboarding.
Notes: Only ever writes files after you explicitly say okay, and only inside the onboarding-output/ folder — it won't touch anything else. Every comprehension check is now a quick click, not typing. If a prior session exists, it offers a refresher or a resume instead of always starting over — and if you run out of time or confidence mid-session, it saves your place to onboarding-output/onboarding-progress.md so you can pick up right where you left off.

Purpose: A deeper, more thorough version of onboarding for people who are completely new to Claude Code or non-technical — it doesn't finish until you can work on your own. If you've already done /start, it can shortcut the basics and move straight to the deeper, role-specific material; if not, it works perfectly well on its own.
When to Use: Say things like I am new here
Where to Use: this is my first task
How to Use: or I don't understand MCP" — use this one if Start feels too quick."
Input Requirements: Formal onboarding for a new employee, especially before their first real task.
Expected Output: Type /new-joinee, optionally followed by your role or first task (e.g. /new-joinee support agent). (See the install guide below: needs to be saved to the right folder first.)
Status: Your name, role, first assigned task, and whether you've used tools like this before. You'll also be asked to say yes before anything gets saved.
Version: A full teaching session that ends with two short checks, plus a short list of specific skills recommended for your role. Pass both checks and you also get a completion certificate — everything saved under onboarding-output/.
Notes: Testing
column14: Fixed: allowed-tools now includes Write (frontmatter can't scope Write by path, so the skill's own Guardrails restrict it to onboarding-output/ only, same pattern /start uses). The certificate and cheat-sheet templates are now inlined directly in Step 14 instead of linking to a templates/ folder that never existed. If you've already completed /start, it checks for that first and offers to shorten the basics recap instead of starting over.

Purpose: Helps you create a brand-new Claude skill from scratch, or review and improve one that already exists.
When to Use: Whenever you want to build a new skill, clean up an existing one, or aren't sure if a skill is set up well.
Where to Use: Anywhere skills are being written or maintained for this project.
How to Use: Type /skill-builder, or just say you want to create or improve a skill. It asks a short series of questions first before writing anything. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Answers to a short back-and-forth: what the skill should do, what triggers it, and what it should never do. Skips questions you've already answered up front.
Expected Output: A new or improved skill file, following the project's standard quality checklist.
Notes: One thing to know: it links out to a file called reference.md, but in this repository that file is actually named reference_skill_builder.md, so the link doesn't resolve as written.

Purpose: Gives you a guided, read-only tour of an unfamiliar project — what it's for, how it's organized, and what's safe to try first.
When to Use: Ask for a tour, ask Claude to explain what's in a project, or say you want to understand a codebase before touching it.
Where to Use: The very start of working in any project you haven't seen before.
How to Use: Type /project-discovery, optionally with a folder path. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Nothing required — just point it at a project, or let it use the current one.
Expected Output: A plain-language summary in chat: what the project does, its folders, what skills exist, what's connected, and one safe first step. It never creates any files.
Notes: Fixed: allowed-tools now scopes Bash to exactly the three commands the skill's own instructions describe (git status, git branch --show-current, git log --oneline -5) instead of granting unrestricted Bash — previously flagged as an inconsistency. Also now runs as a forked Explore subagent (context: fork) since it's self-contained and doesn't need conversation history.

Purpose: Checks whether something similar already exists before you build it from scratch — saves you from accidentally duplicating work.
When to Use: Before creating any new file, report, script, dashboard, or skill — or any time you're not sure if this already exists somewhere.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right before starting new work.
How to Use: Type /existing-asset-finder followed by a short description of what you're about to build. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A short description of the thing you're thinking of building — a name, a purpose, or even a rough idea is enough to start.
Expected Output: A short report recommending REUSE, EXTEND, MERGE, CREATE, or STOP, with the evidence behind that call.
Notes: It only looks, never touches anything — it won't create, change, or delete a single file, even if it recommends doing so. Acting on it is always up to you.

Purpose: Turns a fuzzy, half-formed task (“I need to do X but I'm not sure how”) into a clear, honest plan — showing exactly what's confirmed and what's still a guess.
When to Use: Whenever a request feels vague or you're not sure where to start — especially useful for your first few tasks in a new role.
Where to Use: Right at the start of any unclear task, before you dive in.
How to Use: Type /first-task-mapper followed by your task, or just describe it and answer the follow-up questions. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A description of the task, then a short back-and-forth: the actual goal, where the data comes from, who reviews the result, and so on.
Expected Output: A clear one-page plan in chat, with every detail labelled Confirmed, Assumption, or Unknown, plus a readiness verdict. Saves to a file only if you ask.
Notes: Important: it only plans the work, it never does the task itself — and it won't guess at things like who should review the result; it marks those “not confirmed” instead. Every clarifying question is now a quick click, not typing (you can still type a custom answer via “Other”).

Purpose: Reviews a set of requirements or a project brief and flags anything missing, unclear, or contradictory before work starts on it.
When to Use: Before development begins on a document, ticket, or brief that feels incomplete or ambiguous.
Where to Use: Any pre-development review of requirements or acceptance criteria.
How to Use: Type /requirements-validator followed by a file path, or paste the requirements directly. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The requirements themselves — a file, a ticket, or pasted text. Background like business goals is optional but helpful.
Expected Output: A clear review in chat: what's missing, what's ambiguous, improved acceptance criteria, and any open questions still needing an answer.
Notes: Sticks strictly to what's actually written — it won't invent a requirement that isn't there, and won't rewrite your whole document unless that's genuinely needed for clarity.

Purpose: Cleans up messy Markdown formatting — inconsistent headings, mismatched bullet styles, broken tables — without changing a word of your actual content.
When to Use: Whenever a Markdown file looks messy or inconsistent and needs polishing before it's shared.
Where to Use: Any Markdown document that needs a formatting pass before review or publishing.
How to Use: Type /markdown-document-formatter followed by a file path, or paste the raw Markdown directly. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A Markdown file path, or the raw Markdown text pasted in.
Expected Output: A cleaned-up copy saved next to the original (only after you confirm), named [original-name]-formatted.md, plus a short summary of exactly what was fixed.
Notes: Only fixes formatting and structure — never touches your original file, and never rewrites, shortens, or reworks your actual wording. Shows you the cleaned version and a summary of fixes first, and only saves it after you say okay.

Purpose: Turns rough meeting notes into a clean, structured summary — attendees, decisions, action items with owners, and anything still unresolved.
When to Use: Right after a meeting, whenever you need notes turned into something shareable.
Where to Use: Any post-meeting follow-up or decision tracking.
How to Use: Type /meeting-note-summariser followed by a topic or date, then paste in your notes (or give a file path). (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Your raw meeting notes, pasted in or as a file — a title or date is optional.
Expected Output: A tidy summary shown right in chat by default. It only saves a file if you specifically ask it to.
Notes: Never invents an attendee, decision, or deadline that wasn't actually in your notes — anything unclear is labelled “TBD” instead of guessed at.

Purpose: Drafts a polite, on-brand reply to a customer email — about an order, a refund, a delivery issue, or a general question — for you to review before sending.
When to Use: Whenever a customer email needs a reply drafted for you to check over.
Where to Use: Customer support conversations, before a human sends the final reply.
How to Use: Type /customer-email-reply-drafter and paste in the customer's email. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The customer's email content — a name, order number, or issue type helps but isn't required.
Expected Output: A ready-to-review draft reply in plain text, with clear placeholders (like [insert tracking number]) anywhere information is missing.
Notes: Never invents order or refund details it doesn't have, and never sends the email itself — sending is always a human decision.

Purpose: Turns a product name and a list of features into a polished, ready-to-publish product description.
When to Use: Whenever a new product listing needs description copy written.
Where to Use: E-commerce content prep, before a listing goes live.
How to Use: Type /product-description-writer followed by the product name, then give it the feature list. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The product name plus its features or specs, as a list. A preferred tone or target length is optional.
Expected Output: A polished title (if needed) and a finished description, in plain text or simple Markdown, ready to paste straight into a listing.
Notes: Uses Digitweb Lanka's standard tone — clear, benefit-led, UK English — and never makes up a product detail it wasn't given.

Purpose: Reads an orders CSV and gives you the headline numbers: total orders, total revenue, and your top 3 best-selling products.
When to Use: Whenever you need a quick revenue and top-seller snapshot from an orders export.
Where to Use: Basic order and revenue reporting for e-commerce.
How to Use: Type /order-summary-report followed by the path to your CSV. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: An orders CSV with an order ID, an order total, and a product name or item column.
Expected Output: A plain-text summary: total orders, total revenue, and your top 3 products by quantity — plus a note on any rows it had to skip and why.
Notes: Read-only — never edits your CSV, and never makes up a number it can't actually calculate from the data.

Purpose: Reads an orders CSV and sorts every order into a clear status bucket — delivered, cancelled, on time, or delayed — so you can spot problems fast.
When to Use: Whenever you need to check delivery status across a batch of orders, especially to catch delays.
Where to Use: Order operations and delivery monitoring.
How to Use: Type /order-status-summary followed by the path to your CSV. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: An orders CSV with order ID, customer name, order date, ship date, expected delivery date, and status columns.
Expected Output: Counts for each status bucket, plus a table of delayed orders sorted worst-first, so the most overdue ones are easy to spot.
Notes: If a required column is missing, it stops and asks you to fix the file rather than guessing at the answer.

Purpose: Compares a task you're about to do against every skill already in this project and tells you exactly what to do with it — reuse a skill as-is, reuse it with different inputs, combine a few, extend one, build something new, or hand the call to a human.
When to Use: Whenever you're not sure which skill fits a task, or want to check whether you actually need to build something new before you start.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right before deciding how to tackle a new task.
How to Use: Type /skill-finder followed by a description of the task. If that's too vague
Input Requirements: it'll ask one quick follow-up question first.
Expected Output: A short description of the task you're trying to do — the more specific, the better the comparison.
Status: A short report in chat: which skills it considered, how each one compares, and one clear recommendation with the reasoning behind it. It also flags if CLAUDE.md's skill list doesn't match what's actually on disk.
Notes: Version 1.0
Files: Read-only and chat-only — it never creates, edits, or deletes any skill file, and never saves its report anywhere. It only recommends; acting on that recommendation (building, extending, or combining skills) is always a separate request.

Purpose: Stress-tests any plan, design, or decision — a new skill idea, an architecture choice, a process change — by asking one question at a time, each with a recommended answer, until every decision, dependency, assumption, risk, and branch is nailed down.
When to Use: Say things like “grill me on this,” “stress-test this plan or idea,” “poke holes in this,” or “make sure I've thought of everything” — anytime you're about to commit to something that hasn't been fully thought through.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right before committing to a plan, design, or decision — pairs naturally before /skill-builder's own discovery interview, but isn't limited to skills.
How to Use: Type /grill-me followed by the plan or topic, or just say you want it grilled and point at what's being discussed — Claude will use whatever's already in the conversation if you don't specify a topic.
Input Requirements: A plan, idea, or design to interrogate — given as an argument, or just whatever's currently being discussed. Nothing else needed to start.
Expected Output: A one-question-at-a-time interview in chat, each with a recommended answer you can pick with one click — tracked as a visible task list until every open item is resolved. Ends with a structured summary of every decision made; no file is written unless you ask.
Notes: Never builds or implements anything itself, even once the plan becomes fully clear — it only interrogates and hands back a resolved plan as a separate follow-up. If the open-items list grows past roughly 15-20, it pauses to suggest splitting the plan into smaller pieces instead of continuing indefinitely.

Purpose: Builds a reusable, traceable evidence pack for completed work — task brief, source references, queries/scripts, raw extracts, validation results, screenshots, assumptions, limitations, a decision log, and a final-output reference, all in one auditable folder.
When to Use: Say things like “build an evidence pack for this,” “document proof of this work,” “compile the evidence for this task,” or “I need a paper trail for this” — anytime completed work needs organized, traceable proof.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right after finishing a task that needs an audit trail — works the same way for any department or task type.
How to Use: Type /evidence-pack-builder followed by the task or topic, or just ask for an evidence pack — Claude uses whatever was just completed in the conversation if you don't specify a topic.
Input Requirements: A completed task to document — as an argument, or just whatever was just finished in the conversation. Any gaps (like screenshot file paths) are asked for directly.
Expected Output: A new output/evidence-packs/<task-slug>/ folder with a README.md index plus one file per component, each marked Available, Not provided, or Not applicable — never fabricated.
Notes: Never modifies the original source/task files it documents — only reads from and copies into the pack. Redacts credentials, secrets, and personal/sensitive information before writing anything, and keeps raw evidence strictly separate from analysis, with every conclusion linked to the raw file(s) that support it.

Purpose: Teaches beginners how MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects Claude to real company systems, using one interactive, explorable diagram — verifies connector availability where possible and explains data access, permissions, and ownership.
When to Use: Ask things like “how does MCP work,” “what can Claude access,” “explain our connectors,” “onboard me to MCP,” or “do I have access to X.”
Where to Use: Anywhere someone needs to understand what Claude can actually reach in this project and why — especially useful early on, alongside /start.
How to Use: Type /mcp-access-guide, or just ask how MCP or your connectors work — Claude checks what's actually live in the session before answering.
Input Requirements: Nothing required to start. If you ask about a specific connector, it re-checks live availability before answering rather than relying on memory.
Expected Output: One interactive Artifact (a clickable diagram: User → Claude → MCP Server → Company System → Data) plus a connector panel, walked through conversationally. Every connector status is labeled exactly Live verified, Registry verified, Demo only — Needs confirmation, or Installed — Not authenticated.
Notes: Never stores or displays secrets, and never modifies configuration, connections, or permissions — teaching and diagnosis only. Demo/simulated connectors are always clearly labeled as such, never presented as real results.

Purpose: Checks whether a task is genuinely ready to close — nine areas verified against real evidence before it's marked done.
When to Use: Say things like “is this ready to close,” “can we close this out,” or “verify this is done” — anytime before marking a task complete.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right at the end of any task — before committing, publishing, or reporting something as finished.
How to Use: Type /task-closure, optionally followed by the task name — or just ask if it's ready to close and Claude will use whatever was just completed in the conversation.
Input Requirements: A task or topic name — as an argument, or just whatever was just finished in the conversation. If it's not clear which task, Claude asks first rather than guessing.
Expected Output: A structured report in chat: a table tracing each original requirement to its evidence, nine dimension checks (requirements, deliverables, validation, assumptions, evidence, approvals, temporary files, unresolved issues, handoff), and exactly one closure decision — COMPLETE, COMPLETE WITH LIMITATIONS, REVIEW REQUIRED, BLOCKED, or INCOMPLETE.
Notes: Never modifies, publishes, or deletes anything without asking first, action by action — including cleaning up leftover temporary files. Never marks anything Confirmed without real evidence behind it, and never treats silence as confirmation that nothing's outstanding. Pairs with /first-task-mapper and /evidence-pack-builder as the closing check of a task.

Purpose: A hands-on, one-topic-at-a-time lesson in the physical mechanics of using VS Code and Claude Code — not the conceptual architecture start/new-joinee teach, but the actual buttons, panels, and prompts a beginner is looking at.
When to Use: Type /claude-code-basics directly — it doesn't auto-trigger from conversation, so point a beginner to it explicitly once they need the how-do-I-actually-use-this-thing basics.
Where to Use: Anywhere a total beginner needs to learn VS Code + Claude Code mechanics — opening a folder, the Explorer, the panel, slash commands, the terminal, and reviewing edits — before or alongside /start.
How to Use: Type /claude-code-basics. Works through nine topics one at a time, each with a short explanation, a demo where possible, a small exercise, and a comprehension check you have to actually pass before moving on.
Input Requirements: Nothing needed to start — a quick self-assessment lets you skip topics you already know. You can pause, repeat, ask for another example, or stop at any point.
Expected Output: A guided, interactive lesson in chat — including two real, live permission prompts (creating and editing a practice file) so you experience the actual Accept/Reject UI, not just a description of it. Optionally saves a cheat sheet to onboarding-output/ at the end.
Notes: Deliberately excludes Write and Edit from its own pre-approved tools, so every file operation in the lesson triggers a genuine approval prompt for you to practice on. Can't demonstrate UI-only topics like the Explorer directly since Claude can't see your screen — those rely on you describing what you see instead. Complements, not replaces, /start and /new-joinee.

Purpose: Guides an employee through creating, reviewing, editing, and safely maintaining one verified daily status entry per work date, plus first-time setup and a self-attested admin identity correction.
When to Use: Whenever an employee needs to record today's (or a past) work update, check whether today's entry is complete, or correct a wrong name/ID on file. Triggers on natural language (“record my daily work”, “update today's tracker”) or by typing /daily-work-tracker directly.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project when tracking daily work status is needed — typically once per workday.
How to Use: Type /daily-work-tracker, optionally followed by an action: today / a date / view [date] / edit [date] / setup / status [date] / admin-update-identity. First-time use triggers guided setup.
Input Requirements: Employee name and ID (first-time setup only); per entry: working times, completed work, work in progress, blockers, evidence/notes, next actions — conversational or pasted.
Expected Output: A verified Markdown entry saved to output/daily-work-tracker/<employee-id>/<year>/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md, with a completion status report. Weekday-only; leave/holiday days are employee-declared. Reminder automation is a documented future phase, not implemented.
Notes: Uses three PowerShell helper scripts for deterministic state — the only skill in this repo with executable scripts. admin-update-identity is self-attestation + audit-log, not a real authorization check.

Purpose: Turns evidence of a demonstrated workflow — or a live guided walkthrough — into a confirmed, reusable workflow specification: stable rules separated from runtime data, decisions/dependencies/approvals/exceptions/validation requirements identified, every material item tagged with provenance and confidence, then handed to skill-builder to build or extend the actual skill.
When to Use: Whenever you have evidence of a workflow (transcripts, screenshots, event logs, example inputs/outputs, SOPs, or an existing skill to update) — or want to teach Claude a process live, one stage at a time — and want it captured as a durable, reusable skill instead of a one-off result. User-invocation only: type /record-a-skill directly; Claude never auto-triggers this from natural language.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project when a demonstrated or described workflow should become a proper, reusable Claude Code skill.
How to Use: Type /record-a-skill, optionally followed by a workflow name and/or an evidence file path. Confirms an intake mode (pre-processed evidence, live guided walkthrough, or both), screens evidence for sensitive content, reconstructs the workflow with provenance/confidence tagging, asks for explicit project-or-personal scope, delegates an overlap check to existing-asset-finder, then hands the confirmed specification to skill-builder — with a confirmation gate before every persistent write.
Input Requirements: Evidence of a demonstrated workflow (transcripts, screenshots, event logs, example input/output files, SOPs/checklists, or an existing skill for an update) and/or a live typed walkthrough. Raw video/audio files aren't supported — convert to a supported format first.
Expected Output: A confirmed output/record-a-skill/<task-slug>/workflow-specification.md (with supporting analysis/ and raw/ folders), and — once approved — a new or extended skill built by skill-builder. Nothing is committed or pushed to Git automatically.
Notes: Delegates overlap discovery to existing-asset-finder and final skill construction/testing to skill-builder — never edits a target skill directly. Screens evidence across three layers (pattern rules, semantic review, user confirmation) before any write; raw evidence and staging artifacts are git-ignored and never become runtime dependencies of the generated skill.

Purpose: Scaffolds the exact, frozen AIS-OS starter-kit folder structure into an empty target directory, then cryptographically verifies the result before reporting success. Portable and self-contained — all template content and its verification manifest ship inside the skill's own folder.
When to Use: Whenever you need a brand-new project seeded with the frozen AIS-OS baseline structure. User-invocation only: type /aios-structure-build directly; Claude never auto-triggers this from natural language.
Where to Use: In an empty target directory (tolerates only pre-existing sibling aios-structure-* skill folders under .claude/skills/) — works installed personally or project-locally with no changes.
How to Use: Type /aios-structure-build. Runs the bundled build.ps1: preflight-verifies every template's SHA-256 against manifest.json, confirms the target is empty, writes the baseline tree, re-verifies every written file's hash, then reports. Any failure triggers automatic rollback of only what that attempt created.
Input Requirements: None beyond an empty (or near-empty) target directory.
Expected Output: The full frozen AIS-OS baseline tree (9 directories, 14 files) written to the target, with a created/preserved report and a hard pass/fail verification result.
Notes: Sibling of aios-structure-organize (repairs) and aios-structure-validate (read-only check) — only ever targets a fresh, empty directory. Never touches git or registers itself in the scaffolded project's frozen CLAUDE.md/decisions log.

Purpose: Additively repairs an existing AIS-OS project by creating whatever's missing against the frozen starter-kit baseline, via a dry-run plan followed by explicit confirmation. Never overwrites, deletes, or moves anything that already exists.
When to Use: Whenever an existing AIS-OS project is missing baseline files or directories and you want them restored without touching anything already present. User-invocation only: type /aios-structure-organize directly; Claude never auto-triggers this from natural language.
Where to Use: In an existing AIS-OS project only — redirects (exit 2) if no AIS-OS identifying files are found. Works installed personally or project-locally with no changes.
How to Use: Type /aios-structure-organize. Runs organize.ps1 without -Apply first for a dry-run plan of what's missing; confirms with you via AskUserQuestion; only on explicit yes, re-runs with -Apply to create the missing items. Never skips the dry-run -> confirm -> apply sequence.
Input Requirements: An existing AIS-OS project (detected via 7 distinctive baseline files). One explicit yes/no confirmation before anything is written.
Expected Output: Only the missing baseline items get created — existing files, even if drifted, are left completely untouched. Reparse-point collisions reported as blocked, not silently written through.
Notes: Highest-risk sibling — the only one writing to an already-in-use project. Deliberately narrower than validate's full issue set (missing items only, never drift/anti-patterns). Never touches git.

Purpose: Read-only structural check of an existing AIS-OS project against the frozen starter-kit baseline — reports missing items, structural drift, non-empty placeholders, and anti-pattern clutter, each with a concrete manual fix. Not a maturity score (see /audit for that, if installed).
When to Use: Whenever you want to check whether an AIS-OS project's file tree literally matches the frozen baseline, without changing anything. User-invocation only: type /aios-structure-validate directly; Claude never auto-triggers this from natural language.
Where to Use: In an existing AIS-OS project only — redirects (exit 2) if no AIS-OS identifying files are found. Works installed personally or project-locally with no changes.
How to Use: Type /aios-structure-validate. Runs validate.ps1: preflight-verifies its own bundled templates, scans the target against the baseline, then reports categorized issues. Optionally offers to save the report to validations/validate-{date}.md on explicit consent.
Input Requirements: An existing AIS-OS project (detected via 7 distinctive baseline files). One optional yes/no consent if you want the report saved.
Expected Output: A PASS message, or a categorized report (Missing / Structural Drift / Non-Empty Placeholders / Unrecognized Items), each with a concrete fix line. Never flags content-mutable files for content changes.
Notes: Sibling of build (fresh scaffold) and organize (additive repair) — only ever reads, with one optional consented report write. Never deep-recurses into node_modules/, .git/, or growth-folder internals.
